newsitem.title: AUSTRIA: Lessons from Iraq spur IAEA to tougher inspections.
newsitem.headline: Lessons from Iraq spur IAEA to tougher inspections.

text.p: The world's atomic watchdog agency, spurred by what it called "the lessons learnt in Iraq", on Friday launched a tougher regime of nuclear inspections to try to sniff out attempts by nations to build nuclear arms.

The executive board of governors of the U.N.'s International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) approved the new measures after five years of negotiations among more than 130 member nations of the Vienna-based organisation.
"The measures signify a leap forward to stronger, more effective safeguards," IAEA director-general Hans Blix of Sweden told a news conference.

"A good deal of what we are now doing is based on the lessons learnt in Iraq...That Iraq was able to build up an enrichment capacity and design a nuclear weapon proved our safeguards system did not give us enough access to enable discovery," he added.

In a message read out at the board meeting on Thursday, President Bill Clinton said: "The United States stands ready to apply the new measures as fully as possible in our country consistent with our obligations under the NPT (nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty)."
Washington's ambassador to the IAEA, John Ritch, told reporters the new measures were an enormous step forward and represented a necessary complement to the NPT.
"Ironically, this achievement stems from the treachery of (Iraqi President) Saddam Hussein. It will be his only positive legacy," he said.
The other four declared nuclear weapons states, Russia, China, Britain and France were prepared to go some way to accepting the new inspections as a sign of goodwill, IAEA sources said.
But Moscow and Beijing were believed not to have given much ground on allowing widespread access to nuclear sites.

Representatives of the so-called "nuclear threshold states", Israel, India and Pakistan, which have not signed the NPT, made clear at talks that the new protocol would not apply to them, diplomatic sources said.
"But Israel has not slammed the door shut," one Western diplomat said.
IAEA officials expect member nations to begin signing the protocol by the end of the year. Some countries have to submit the new measures for ratification by their parliaments.
The agency, set up 40 years ago, took on a more high-profile monitoring role in the wake of the NPT, checking compliance with safeguards provisions.
But inspectors were allowed to check only those nuclear sites declared by an IAEA member and had to give lengthy notice of a visit, allowing time for the concealment of any undesirable evidence.
Following the Gulf War in 1991, the agency was genuinely shocked, not to say embarrassed, to discover that Baghdad had been developing a nuclear arms programme.
IAEA inspectors had checked some sites in Iraq before its invasion of Kuwait in 1990, but were not allowed near other non-declared areas.
Suspicions in 1993 that North Korea had similar intentions were a second sharp reminder that IAEA surveillance was limited.
The guidelines set out in a new protocol give IAEA inspectors the authority to check any non-declared installations, especially research and development facilities.
Inspectors need only to give 24-hours notice to visit a site and in exceptional circumstances an expert working on-site can ask to see an installation immediately.

State-of-the-art technology will be used to collect soil, water and other samples, analyse them and check the level of radioactive activity against the nuclear programme reports submitted by a nation.
Nuclear inspectors will be able to communicate by satellite with the database in Vienna to file their reports home, saving the time and expense of travelling back and forth from IAEA headquarters.
Remote surveillance of sites will be set up, feeding information directly into IAEA computers in Vienna.
Asked whether the new measures would mean that a similar case to Iraq could never happen again, Blix said:
"We cannot get to 100 percent certainty...but this should enable us to have a better chance of seeing the smoke."
